entries.answer: Lungsod means city, and in the Philippines it is a term with a legal meaning rather than just a word for a big town. Under the charter system a city is one that has met population, income and land requirements and been granted that status by Congress, and the city as a separate corporate entity is what allows it to run its own schools, police, health and revenue. That is why a city and a municipality in the same province can have very different powers, and why a city does not belong to the province the way a municipality does. Quezon City, the largest by population, is not part of Metro Manila in the way people assume, since it was never part of Rizal province, while the other sixteen cities of Metro Manila are. The word covers both the legal city and the everyday idea of a large town, and the second sense is the one a visitor usually means.

entries.answer: Barangay is the smallest administrative unit in the Philippines, and it is the word a newcomer meets almost immediately because it is the basic unit of government below the city or municipality. Its head is the barangay captain, elected every three years, and the council passes local ordinances on matters such as health, cleanliness, the market and the naming of streets. What it does not do is handle matters that belong to higher levels: national defence, taxation and most of education sit with other agencies, which is why a barangay cannot be asked to fix a national problem. The word comes from the Spanish barangay, a boat with outriggers, and is also used informally for a neighbourhood or a group of neighbours, so saying the barangay can mean a place or the people in it. It is the level where community programmes such as the health centre and the youth and sports programmes actually operate.
